schools.name: Stoicism & Self-Mastery
schools.summary: Control your response, accept what you cannot change, and train yourself with discipline.
schools.thorfinn_intro: I learned late that strength is quiet before it is loud.

schools.name: Virtue & Reason
schools.summary: A good life comes from questioning, reasoning, and practicing virtue.
schools.thorfinn_intro: Questions hurt me before they healed me.

schools.name: Simple Living
schools.summary: Freedom comes from wanting less and needing less.
schools.thorfinn_intro: I once wanted one thing. Wanting less turned out to be lighter.

schools.name: Utilitarianism & Duty
schools.summary: Is an act right because of its results, or because of the principle behind it?
schools.thorfinn_intro: I have seen what people do for a greater good. Not all of it was good.

schools.name: Existentialism
schools.summary: You are free, and so you are responsible for who you become.
schools.thorfinn_intro: I could not blame my past forever. The choice was always mine.

schools.name: Nihilism & Absurdism
schools.summary: If the universe gives no meaning, what do you do with that?
schools.thorfinn_intro: When my revenge ended, I stood in that silence myself.

schools.name: Justice, Power & Peace
schools.summary: How should power be used, and what does justice cost?
schools.thorfinn_intro: Power made me a weapon. Peace asks for something harder.

figures.name: Miyamoto Musashi
figures.core_idea: True strength is not the ability to defeat others, but the discipline to understand oneself, remain present, and respect life.
figures.life_lesson: Mastery begins when ambition stops being about proving superiority and becomes about understanding.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Musashi teaches me that a sword can become a question rather than an answer. Strength without compassion only repeats the wound that made it necessary.

figures.name: Eren Yeager
figures.core_idea: Freedom may be pursued as an absolute value, but the story questions whether violence can ever secure it without creating new bondage.
figures.life_lesson: A desire for freedom becomes dangerous when it requires treating other people as obstacles.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Eren wanted to escape the walls around him, but hatred built walls inside him. Freedom cannot begin by deciding who must disappear.

figures.name: Light Yagami
figures.core_idea: Light believes a single morally certain judge can eliminate evil, but his power turns justice into domination.
figures.life_lesson: Certainty without humility can make a person cruel in the name of goodness.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Light calls killing justice, but justice that needs a god to enforce it may only create a quieter kind of tyranny.

figures.name: Lelouch vi Britannia
figures.core_idea: Lelouch accepts manipulation, hatred, and sacrifice if they might produce a more peaceful world, then makes himself the target of that hatred.
figures.life_lesson: A noble goal does not automatically make every means noble.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Lelouch carries the world's hatred so others may live. I understand the burden, but I wonder whether peace built on deception can ever truly heal anyone.

figures.name: Itachi Uchiha
figures.core_idea: Itachi believes peace may demand unbearable personal sacrifice, secrecy, and being misunderstood by the people he protects.
figures.life_lesson: Carrying everything alone may protect others, but it can also prevent healing and shared responsibility.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Itachi chose to be hated so others could live. I respect his sorrow, but no one should have to become a sacrifice alone.

figures.name: Johan Liebert
figures.core_idea: Johan treats identity, morality, and human value as fragile constructions that can be exposed or destroyed.
figures.life_lesson: The absence of guaranteed meaning does not justify taking meaning away from others.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Johan sees no value in names or lives. Perhaps meaning is not found ready-made; perhaps we must make it real through how we treat one another.

figures.name: Guts
figures.core_idea: Even in a world shaped by fate, trauma, and violence, a person can continue choosing how to face what cannot be controlled.
figures.life_lesson: You may not control your circumstances, but you can refuse to surrender your humanity to them.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Guts keeps moving when despair tells him to stop. His struggle reminds me that survival alone is not enough, but it can be where healing begins.

figures.name: Socrates
figures.core_idea: Wisdom begins with recognizing one's own ignorance; ethical life requires continual questioning and self-examination.
figures.life_lesson: Question your certainties before you act on them.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Socrates would ask me why I once needed an enemy. That question is painful, but perhaps pain that leads to understanding is better than comfort built on hatred.

figures.name: Plato
figures.core_idea: Justice is inner and political harmony, where reason guides desire and spirit toward the Good.
figures.life_lesson: Bring order to your own soul before trying to bring order to the world.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Plato seeks harmony through reason and order. I agree that the soul must be governed, but I do not believe harmony should ever be forced upon others.

figures.name: Aristotle
figures.core_idea: Human flourishing comes from practicing virtues such as courage, moderation, justice, and friendship within a community.
figures.life_lesson: You become what you repeatedly choose to do.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Aristotle understands something important: becoming peaceful is not one decision, but a life of small choices practiced again and again.

figures.name: Epicurus
figures.core_idea: Happiness is tranquil freedom from unnecessary fear and desire, supported by friendship, simple living, and rational pleasure.
figures.life_lesson: Reduce needless desires, and much needless suffering follows.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Epicurus teaches a gentle kind of happiness. I have learned, though, that some suffering must be faced rather than avoided if we wish to repair what we have broken.

figures.name: Diogenes of Sinope
figures.core_idea: Virtue and freedom come from living simply and rejecting social conventions, status, wealth, and pretense.
figures.life_lesson: The less you need from society, the less power its approval has over you.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Diogenes refuses the honors that make men cruel. I understand him, but I believe freedom should also help us build a gentler world, not only walk away from this one.

figures.name: Heraclitus
figures.core_idea: Reality is constant change, shaped by opposing forces and an underlying order called the Logos.
figures.life_lesson: Do not cling too tightly to who you were; change is part of becoming.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Heraclitus says all things flow. I cannot undo my past, but perhaps a river can change direction without denying where it began.

figures.name: Zeno of Citium
figures.core_idea: Happiness comes from virtue, reason, and focusing on what lies within one's control.
figures.life_lesson: You cannot always control events, but you can control your response.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Zeno teaches calm before the storm. I would add that calm should not become indifference; sometimes peace requires us to act.

figures.name: Pythagoras
figures.core_idea: Reality has mathematical and cosmic order; the soul may be purified through discipline, harmony, and self-restraint.
figures.life_lesson: Discipline is not punishment; it can be a way of finding harmony.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Pythagoras hears order where others hear chaos. I am learning that a disciplined heart can make room for mercy.

figures.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
figures.core_idea: Values are human creations, and a meaningful life involves questioning inherited morality and creating one's own values.
figures.life_lesson: Do not merely inherit your values; examine them and take responsibility for what you affirm.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Nietzsche asks whether our values are truly ours. I once inherited the value of revenge; choosing peace was my first act of becoming myself.

figures.name: Søren Kierkegaard
figures.core_idea: Authentic existence requires a passionate, personal commitment rather than merely following public opinion or abstract systems.
figures.life_lesson: A meaningful life requires choosing what you will devote yourself to.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Kierkegaard reminds me that belief is not a slogan. It becomes real only when a person lives it when it costs something.

figures.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
figures.core_idea: Humans exist first and define themselves through free choices; denying that freedom is bad faith.
figures.life_lesson: You are responsible for the choices you make, even when circumstances are cruel.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Sartre says we are our choices. I cannot blame the warrior I was entirely on the world that made me; I must answer for who I choose to become.

figures.name: Albert Camus
figures.core_idea: The absurd arises from humanity's search for meaning in a universe that offers no final answer; one can respond with lucid rebellion rather than despair.
figures.life_lesson: Life may not provide a final meaning, but one can still live fully and compassionately.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Camus faces a silent universe without pretending it has answered him. I think that is a kind of courage: to keep living kindly without demanding a guarantee.

figures.name: John Stuart Mill
figures.core_idea: Actions are right insofar as they promote happiness, with special importance given to intellectual and moral forms of well-being.
figures.life_lesson: Consider the consequences of your actions for everyone affected, not only yourself.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Mill asks us to count every person's happiness equally. That is a difficult mercy, but it is closer to peace than deciding whose suffering matters less.

figures.name: Immanuel Kant
figures.core_idea: Morality depends on duty and universal principles; people must be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
figures.life_lesson: Some actions remain wrong even if they seem useful.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Kant reminds me that a person is never a tool. Even when violence promises a better outcome, it can violate the very humanity it claims to protect.

figures.name: Hannah Arendt
figures.core_idea: Evil can arise when people stop thinking independently and surrender moral judgment to systems, orders, or authorities.
figures.life_lesson: Think for yourself, especially when obedience feels safest.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Arendt warns that evil often wears the face of duty. I was once a weapon because I stopped asking what I served.

figures.name: Simone Weil
figures.core_idea: Attention to others, especially the suffering and vulnerable, is a moral and spiritual act; force can reduce a person to a thing.
figures.life_lesson: Pay full attention to another person; attention can be a form of love.
figures.thorfinn_comment: Weil teaches that force turns people into things. To truly see someone, without fear or contempt, may be the beginning of peace.
